title: Korea’s September report links its rate hikes to the spillover from semiconductor income
summary: The Bank of Korea’s September Monetary Policy Report explained two consecutive summer rate increases by reference to a stronger domestic economy, inflation persistence and financial stability risks. The English edition was posted on 16 November. It describes conditions from March through August and uses the August forecast vintage. The Board held the Base Rate at 2.50% in April and May while assessing the impact of conflict in the Middle East, then raised it by 25 basis points at both the July and August meetings to reach 3.00%. The risk that a semiconductor boom would strengthen domestic demand made it less attractive to wait for an oil-related rise in inflation to unwind (executive summary and chapter II).

In the August outlook, the Bank projected real GDP growth of 3.3% in 2026 and 2.9% in 2027. Exports and investment in information technology had surprised on the upside, consumption was recovering, and the improvement in employment remained more modest. Headline inflation, in the low twos early in the year, had risen to around 3% after the Middle East shock. The Bank expected headline inflation of 2.7% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027, compared with core rates of 2.5% in both years. Falling oil-related pressure could therefore pull headline inflation down even while past cost increases and improving demand sustained underlying prices. More expensive semiconductors could also feed into durable-goods prices (chapter I and figure II-20).

The report’s special analysis separates export income from output volumes. It attributes approximately 15 percentage points of 22% nominal GDP growth in the first half of 2026 to improved terms of trade. Real growth and the domestic demand deflator contributed about 3.8 and 3.1 percentage points respectively. Higher memory-chip prices accounted for much of the export-price gain. Corporate earnings and tax revenue could respond quickly to this windfall. Broader consumption and investment required an additional step, such as greater capital expenditure, wage payments or public spending. Chipmaking’s concentration in a few large employers, weak construction and gaps between smaller and larger firms could limit that transmission. The contrast matters to portfolios exposed to domestic demand as well as to the earnings of exporters (chapter III, figures III-2, III-6 and III-13).

The same denominator effect complicates assessment of household leverage. Rapid nominal income growth could lower household debt relative to GDP while mortgage balances and Seoul-area housing prices continued to rise. A lower national ratio would not establish that new borrowers could service larger loans. With housing supply constrained and buyers still expecting appreciation, the Bank saw a reason to account for financial imbalances when deciding the timing and pace of subsequent policy moves (chapter II, figure II-21 and chapter III, figure III-17).

The August six-month policy projections still allowed for more than one path. Ten of 21 dots were at 3.25%, six were at 3.50% and five were at 3.00%. Seven Board members each submitted three dots to describe their conditional distribution. Counting the ten dots at 3.25% as ten votes, or treating them as probabilities implied by bond prices, would misread the chart. The projections depended on inflation, the semiconductor cycle, the strength of domestic spillovers and housing credit (figures II-22–23 and footnote 114).

The Bank also separated the monetary stance from its market operations. Twenty-four-hour domestic FX trading began in July, while other changes addressed currency liquidity. Plans for the Bank Intermediated Lending Support Facility aimed to improve the credit channel and support regional SMEs. Easier access to particular funding channels could coexist with a higher Base Rate. The report did not establish how much of the conditional policy path investors had already priced or what the Board would decide at meetings after its information cutoff.

questions.question: How widely was the semiconductor income gain passing through to domestic demand?
questions.detail: The report identifies a large terms-of-trade gain but flags concentration in leading manufacturers. Compare export volumes and prices, firms’ actual capital spending, bonuses, employment and household consumption across regions and income groups. The Bank’s national accounts, semiconductor company filings and official wage statistics would help distinguish a durable domestic demand impulse from higher nominal export receipts concentrated among a few firms.

questions.question: Was underlying inflation broadening enough to support further hikes if oil prices stabilised?
questions.detail: Headline and core forecasts diverged, and the report saw scope for higher demand to amplify cost pass-through. Compare monthly price changes in labour-intensive services and non-energy goods with selling-price surveys, wage growth and inflation expectations. Separate semiconductor-intensive durables from other products. The breadth of increases would matter for assessing the persistence of restraint at and beyond the six-month projection horizon.

questions.question: How much housing risk remained after adjusting for unusually rapid nominal GDP growth?
questions.detail: Examine Seoul-area transactions, mortgage originations, debt-service ratios and borrower incomes alongside the national debt-to-GDP ratio. Compare the implied policy distribution with contemporaneous meeting-dated won rates rather than treating the Board’s dots as market evidence. This would help identify whether a position in short rates depends on domestic inflation, concern about housing leverage, or both.
